📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Umamusume clone that uses artwork closely resembling the game’s popular horse girls and racing features has appeared on the Google Play Store, leaving the community wondering how it managed to slip through the net.

From free browser games that combine Pokemon with Umamusume-style races to mods that replace Need for Speed Underground 2’s cars with horse girls, Cygames’ popular mobile game is constantly galloping its way into fan games and community projects.

The anime girl racing game has even sparked an upcoming competitor where players will duke it out against anime girls themed after iconic racing cars.

However, a new game has appeared on the Google Play Store using artwork that closely resembles Umamusume, with players branding it a “shameless” knockoff riddled with ads.

The game in question is Anime Racing Academy, a newly introduced app that was released on November 16 and has over 100 downloads. While there’s no gameplay shown off, developer HIFI PUBLISHERS has uploaded several screenshots of Anime Racing Academy to help give players a feel for what they can expect.

“Get ready for an exciting anime racing adventure in Anime Racing Academy! Experience thrilling racing challenges, compete on exciting tracks, and master your driving skills in this action-packed anime racing game. Enjoy fast-paced gameplay, smooth controls, and exciting racing competition,” reads the game’s official description.

According to recent reports, as you can see from the images below, the game looks eerily similar to Umamusume. There are images of horse girls running full speed across race tracks, idol performances where the characters sing after their victory, and training segments with Uma-style stats shown off.

Umamusume mod perfectly puts anime horse girls into Need for Speed Underground 2.

Umamusume fans can actually race and place bets in latest Steam game.

Umamusume has been transformed into a D&D game with upcoming race.

According to recent reports, some of the anime horse girls themselves also closely resemble Kitasan Black, Oguri Cap, Special Week, and Silence Suzuka. “They’ve got all my favorites: Mejiro McDuke, Commonplace Week, Bronze Ship,” joked one commenter. “That’s not Umamusume, it’s ripoff Musume Bootleg Derby,” added another.

Some players also download the game to see exactly what the “bootleg” version entailed, only to be left shocked by the amount of ads.

It has been revealed that “I had the guts to download and play it. Holy f**king sh*t, what a sh*tty game. There are so many f**king ads that it took five minutes of loading and ads just to get through one race. Brutal,” revealed one player.

Interestingly, the developers have also uploaded another game titled Silver: Open World Detective, which appears to use promotional artwork from the upcoming gacha game Silver Palace.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Steam players will be able to vote for the best game of the past decade as Valve pits previous Game of the Year winners against each other in a latest award category.
  • To celebrate the 10th anniversary of the Steam Awards, Valve has introduced a special Hall of Fame gong for 2026, with the likes of Elden Ring, Baldur’s Gate 3, and GTA 5 all competing against each other.
  • Valve describes the fresh category as “a collection of previous Game of the Year award winners now in competition against each other for the title of #1 game of the past 10 years.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Steam players will be able to vote for the best game of the past decade as Valve pits previous Game of the Year winners against each other in a latest award category.

To celebrate the 10th anniversary of the Steam Awards, Valve has introduced a special Hall of Fame gong for 2026, with the likes of Elden Ring, Baldur’s Gate 3, and GTA 5 all competing against each other.

Valve describes the fresh category as “a collection of previous Game of the Year award winners now in competition against each other for the title of #1 game of the past 10 years.”.

As a dedicated Game of the Year category didn’t exist on the platform until 2018, Valve has confirmed in an FAQ that winners of two other awards will serve as proxies for 2016 and 2017, those being GTA 5 and The Witcher 3.

It’s worth noting that both GTA 5 and The Witcher 3 were originally released in 2013 and 2015, respectively, and these appear to be enhanced and/or remastered versions released later.

Joining them are PUBG (2018), Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice (2019), Red Dead Redemption 2 (2020), Resident Evil Village (2021), Elden Ring (2022), Baldur’s Gate 3 (2023), Black Myth: Wukong (2024), and Hollow Knight: Silksong (2025).

Nominations for the 2026 Steam Awards close on November 30 at 10 AM PT, with voting for the Hall of Fame award set to begin on December 17 alongside Steam’s Winter Sale.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists were left stunned after finding a “surreal” site of kitchen appliances at the bottom of the ocean, all while they thought it was part of a shipwreck.

Oceans are, notoriously, one of the last places on Earth that haven’t been fully explored. The depths of some make it impossible for researchers to actually get a clear picture of what is lurking down there, even with all the money in the world being thrown behind some explorations.

Back in 2017, a group of researchers from NOAA, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, had been using a ROV (remotely operated vehicle) in the Gulf of Mexico while looking for a shipwreck.

However, instead of finding ancient treasure, they stumbled upon a field of kitchen appliances on the seafloor, and couldn’t quite believe it.

In footage only released this year, almost a decade on, scientists from NOAA talked through their findings, with one expert calling it a “bit surreal” to see.

“We are at 1.5km in the deep sea, and here we are moving through a field of chest freezers, fridges, and washing machines,” they added.

Another joked that they’d “return this to the manufacturer and ask about the warranty,” when looking at one of the submerged washing machines.

According to recent reports, the debris had been found as the researchers picked up a “sonar target,” which they suspected to be a shipwreck. Instead, they found a 40-foot-long shipping container with a hole on the outside of it. It is certainly a unique find.

While the fridges and washing machines wouldn’t work on land, they had been put to work under the water, with the scientists finding coral growing on some, and fish also living around them.

Elsewhere, in Italy, divers discovered a 3,300-year-old sword stuck under a lake, and it was in “excellent” condition with a sharp blade too.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • GTA 6’s launch has already drawn a reaction from CD Projekt Red, with Cyberpunk 2’s creative director joking that his own game was “cancelled” after seeing what Rockstar had pulled off.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CD Projekt Red says the jump from The Witcher 3 to The Witcher 4 will be comparable to the one Rockstar made between GTA 5 and GTA 6, with improvements planned for nearly every part of the game.

GTA 6’s launch has already drawn a reaction from CD Projekt Red, with Cyberpunk 2’s creative director joking that his own game was “cancelled” after seeing what Rockstar had pulled off.

However, the comparison came up again during CD Projekt’s earnings call, when the tech giant was asked whether players should expect a similar leap from its next Witcher game.

As first reported by Eurogamer, CD Projekt Red co-CEO Michal Nowakowski mentioned the studio had looked at what changed between Rockstar’s two games and that he expected The Witcher 4 to make a comparable jump.

In a recent development, “We believe there’s going to be a comparable leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4, I think so, yes. It’s been 11 years, we are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game, so yes, you should expect us to make a much bigger jump between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4,” said Nowakowski.

Sources indicate that nowakowski was also asked whether GTA 6’s launch would push CD Projekt Red to spend more on its own games. After all, GTA 6 is expected to have exceeded $1 billion in total development costs.

However, the CD Projekt Red CEO stated the studio’s ambitions for The Witcher 4 and Cyberpunk 2 had stayed the same.

In a recent development, “We have certain ambitions when it comes to Witcher [4] and Cyberpunk 2, they have not changed when it comes to GTA 6. If anything happened as a result of GTA 6, it’s [that it’s] always great to see games like that because they show you how much cool stuff can be done, and that’s for sure an inspiration in many ways for our developers,” he added.

The Witcher 4 dev admits they are worried about living up to Witcher 3.

The Witcher 4 is being developed for PlayStation 5, PC, and Xbox Series X/S and is currently targeting a 2028 launch.

The release also disrupted the world of sports, too. Formula One legend Lewis Hamilton revealed he was hoping to take the day off to play it, while NBA star Steven Adams remarked that sports leagues would “plummet” in quality as a result of GTA 6.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • GTA 6 players who used the Latest Zealand trick to play early on PS5 may have inadvertently purchased a censored version of the game that’s missing a useful stamina buff.
  • With GTA 6 launching at midnight local time on November 19, impatient fans around the world used the Upcoming Zealand trick to get a head start on their adventures in Leonida.
  • While Xbox players could simply change their console’s location, PS5 owners had to create a Newly introduced Zealand PlayStation account and purchase GTA 6 through the country’s digital storefront.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 players who used the Latest Zealand trick to play early on PS5 may have inadvertently purchased a censored version of the game that’s missing a useful stamina buff.

With GTA 6 launching at midnight local time on November 19, impatient fans around the world used the Upcoming Zealand trick to get a head start on their adventures in Leonida.

While Xbox players could simply change their console’s location, PS5 owners had to create a Newly introduced Zealand PlayStation account and purchase GTA 6 through the country’s digital storefront.

Unfortunately, getting into Vice City a few hours early appears to have come with an unexpected drawback.

As reported by IGN, Rockstar left out the ability to consume cocaine from your inventory in the Australian version of GTA 6, with Upcoming Zealand reportedly receiving the same version.

It has been revealed that in the international release, players can collect baggies of cocaine or skim some off larger bricks. Consuming cocaine through the item wheel gives players a supercharged stamina bar for roughly 30 seconds.

Australia’s video game classification rules allow depictions of illicit drug use but prohibit players from receiving gameplay benefits for taking them, even in games rated R18+.

Interestingly, Fresh Zealand doesn’t have this same restriction, but testing by GTA BOOM found that the mechanic was also absent from its New Zealand playthroughs.

Players had already suspected GTA 6 was censored in certain regions before launch when dataminers discovered a roughly 700KB discrepancy in the Australian and New Zealand game files.

Unlike Xbox users who temporarily changed their console’s location, PS5 players who bought the Latest Zealand edition still own that regional copy even when playing on their regular account.

In a recent development, luckily, those affected aren’t missing out on too much. Adrenaline can still be used to boost stamina and other stats, while scripted sequences involving cocaine remain intact.

Still, it’s a rather amusing twist that some of GTA 6‘s most impatient fans ended up with less content than those who waited a few extra hours.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon has responded after one of its delivery drones crashed into a Michigan homeowner’s garage, prompting an investigation by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

The incident occurred on November 20 in Huntington Woods, Michigan, after a couple placed an order for shampoo and received a notification that their package would arrive by drone within seven minutes.

Amazon has been expanding its Prime Air delivery service across the US, aiming to reach nearly 500 cities and towns by the end of 2026. However, several crashes involving its drones have attracted the attention of federal regulators.

Speaking to WXYZ 7 News Detroit, Jim Brennan explained that the drone successfully dropped the package into his backyard before striking a fiber-optic cable and losing one of its propellers.

The aircraft then veered sideways before becoming trapped between his neighbor’s garage roof and nearby power lines.

“Like a sick bird, it tried to go up, it tried to get out of here,” Brennan noted.

Logan Coomes, whose garage was struck, remarked an Amazon Prime Air team arrived within 10 minutes of the crash and worked with local utility workers to remove the drone by early evening.

The firm reportedly offered to help repair the damaged roof and gave Coomes a $100 Amazon gift card.

In a statement shared with CNN, an Amazon spokesperson said its Prime Air drones conduct nearly 6,000 flights per day and have delivered “hundreds of thousands of packages this year.”.

Amazon also said the incident marked the first crash of its kind involving its drone delivery operations near Detroit.

The FAA published a preliminary incident notification on November 23, confirming that it was investigating the crash.

“UAS struck a fiber cable, a residential garage, and became entangled in power lines during takeoff,” the agency noted.

The National Transportation Safety Board is also gathering information but has not yet decided whether to launch a separate investigation.

Amazon’s battery-powered MK30 delivery drones are equipped with technology designed to detect and avoid obstacles and can carry packages weighing up to five pounds.

It has been revealed that the Michigan crash follows several other incidents involving Prime Air. In October 2025, two Amazon delivery drones crashed into a construction crane in Arizona, while another struck an internet cable in Texas the following month.

The FAA has also been investigating a separate crash involving an apartment building in Richardson, Texas, in February 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 16-year-old boy has revealed how a chance encounter in Among Us led to him and his mother helping rescue a teenage girl who had allegedly been held captive for more than 500 days.

Earlier in November, 17-year-old Kylie Arellano was rescued after secretly asking another player for help while playing Innersloth’s popular social deduction game.

Arellano had been missing since May 2025, when she disappeared from her home in Utah at the age of 15. She was allegedly held against her will in the basement of a home in Huntington, Oregon.

For Colorado teenager Landon Tresp, what began as an ordinary gaming session on October 15 would end with him helping a girl hundreds of miles away escape her alleged captor.

After meeting in Among Us, Landon and Arellano struck up a friendship and began communicating through Discord.

“We just kind of clicked,” Landon noted.

Over the following two weeks, Arellano began opening up about her situation, eventually sending Landon news articles covering her disappearance.

Realizing something was seriously wrong, Landon turned to his mother, Khristina, for help on Halloween. Neither knew that within 24 hours, the girl would finally be free.

Khristina began speaking with Arellano through Discord, but locating the teenager proved challenging as she didn’t know the address where she was being held.

“I knew I had to do everything I could to make sure she was brought to safety and had a second chance,” Khristina recalled.

Determined to find her, Khristina searched online property records before turning to real estate website Zillow. After being sent photos of two potential houses, Arellano recognized the second property.

Khristina contacted the girl’s family and began working with the FBI to bring her home.

Speaking with KOAA, Khristina described how devastating it was to learn just how long Arellano had been missing.

“Just heartbreaking to think that she had been going through what she had for over 520 days and without anyone that she could reach a hand out to and not knowing where you’re at,” she remarked.

Sources indicate that on November 1, authorities arrived at the Oregon residence. Khristina stayed on a video call with Arellano, encouraging her to make the final few steps toward freedom.

“I was on the video chat with her when I told her to face those basement stairs and run up them and down that hallway,” Khristina recalled. “And grab that front door because that was her freedom.”.

After more than 500 days away from home, Arellano was finally in the care of law enforcement and was taken for medical treatment and evaluation.

For Landon, seeing the friend he had met just weeks earlier finally reach safety was an overwhelming moment.

Recent findings suggest that “Oh my God, just pure bliss. I was so happy she was safe in that car. I was so happy she was out of that horrible monster’s house,” he said.

Adam Hunter Harmel, 39, has since been indicted on a federal charge of transportation with intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Prosecutors allege he met the girl online before traveling to Utah and taking her across state lines.

Despite everything that happened, Landon and Arellano haven’t stopped playing video games together.

The pair remain friends, while Khristina continues to speak with Arellano every day. The family is also hoping to meet her in person.

#161773. This newly introduced chip survives 1300°F (700°C) and could change AI forever

This newly introduced chip survives 1300°F (700°C) and could change AI forever

📅 07 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1226 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Modern electronics power everything from smartphones to satellites, but they all share a major limitation.
  • Researchers at the University of Southern California now believe they have found a way past that limit.
  • In a study published on March 26, 2026 in Science, a team led by Joshua Yang, Arthur B.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Modern electronics power everything from smartphones to satellites, but they all share a major limitation. Heat. Once temperatures climb above roughly 200 degrees Celsius, most devices begin to break down. For decades, this thermal barrier has been one of the toughest challenges in engineering.

Researchers at the University of Southern California now believe they have found a way past that limit.

In a study published on March 26, 2026 in Science, a team led by Joshua Yang, Arthur B. Freeman Chair Professor at the Ming Hsieh Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the USC Viterbi School of Engineering and the USC School of Advanced Computing, unveiled a new type of memory device that continues to operate at 700 degrees Celsius (~1300 degrees Fahrenheit). That temperature exceeds molten lava and goes far beyond anything previously achieved for this class of technology. The device showed no sign of failure. In fact, 700 degrees was simply the maximum their equipment could test.

"You may call it a revolution," Yang noted. "It is the best high-temperature memory ever demonstrated.".

A Memristor Built for Extreme Heat.

The latest device is known as a memristor, a nanoscale component that can both store data and perform computations. It is constructed like a microscopic layered structure, with two electrodes on either side and a thin ceramic layer in between.

Jian Zhao, the study's first author, built the device using tungsten for the top electrode, hafnium oxide ceramic in the middle, and graphene for the bottom layer. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element, while graphene, a single-atom-thick sheet of carbon, is known for its exceptional strength and heat resistance.

Recent findings suggest that this combination produced remarkable performance. The device retained data for more than 50 hours at 700 degrees without needing to be refreshed. It also endured over one billion switching cycles at that temperature and operated at just 1.5 volts with speeds measured in tens of nanoseconds.

The discovery was not part of the team's original blueprint. They were initially attempting to create a different graphene-based device, which did not work as intended. Along the way, they encountered something surprising.

"To be honest, it was by accident, as most discoveries are," Yang noted. "If you can predict it, it's usually not surprising, and probably not significant enough.".

Further investigation revealed why the device performed so well. In conventional electronics, heat causes metal atoms in the top electrode to slowly migrate through the ceramic layer. Eventually, they reach the bottom electrode, creating a permanent connection that short-circuits the device and leaves it stuck in the on state.

Recent findings suggest that graphene prevents this failure. Its interaction with tungsten is, as Yang described it, similar to oil and water. Tungsten atoms that approach the graphene surface cannot attach to it. Without a stable point to settle, they drift away instead of forming a conductive bridge. This prevents short circuits and preserves the device's function even under extreme heat.

Industry observers note that the researchers confirmed this mechanism using advanced electron microscopy, spectroscopy, and quantum-level simulations. By understanding what happens at the atomic interface, they have turned an unexpected result into a principle that could guide future designs. Other materials with similar surface properties could be identified, which may help scale the technology for industrial production.

Applications in Extreme Environments.

Recent findings suggest that electronics capable of operating above 500 degrees Celsius have long been a goal for space exploration. Venus, for example, has a surface temperature around that level, and every lander sent there has failed in part due to extreme heat. Current silicon-based chips cannot survive such conditions.

"We are now above 700 degrees, and we suspect it will go higher," Yang remarked.

Sources indicate that the potential applications go far beyond space missions. Geothermal energy systems require electronics that can function deep underground, where surrounding rock can glow red-hot. Nuclear and fusion systems also expose equipment to intense heat. Even in everyday settings, durability improves significantly. A device rated for 700 degrees would be extremely robust at the roughly 125-degree temperatures often reached inside automotive electronics.

Why It Matters for Artificial Intelligence.

In a recent development, in addition to storing data, the device offers a major advantage for artificial intelligence. Many AI systems rely heavily on matrix multiplication, a mathematical operation used in tasks like image recognition and language processing. Traditional computers perform these calculations step by step, consuming large amounts of energy.

Memristors approach the problem differently. By using Ohm's Law, where voltage times conductance equals current, the device performs calculations directly as electricity flows through it. The result is obtained instantly as the measured current.

According to recent reports, "Over 92 percent of the computing in AI systems like ChatGPT is nothing but matrix multiplication," Yang said. "This type of device can perform that in the most efficient way, orders of magnitude faster and at lower energy.".

It has been revealed that yang and three co-authors of the study (Qiangfei Xia, Miao Hu, and Ning Ge) have already co-founded a manufacturer called TetraMem to commercialize memristor-based AI chips at room temperature. Their lab is already using working chips from TetraMem for machine learning tasks. The high-temperature version described in this research could extend those capabilities to environments where traditional electronics cannot operate, allowing devices such as spacecraft or industrial sensors to process data directly on site.

From Lab Prototype to Real-World Technology.

Sources indicate that despite the promising results, Yang emphasizes that practical applications are still some distance away. Memory is only one part of a complete computing system. High-temperature logic circuits will also need to be developed and integrated. In addition, the current devices were built manually at very small scales in a laboratory setting, so manufacturing at scale will take time.

According to recent reports, "This is the first step," Yang said. "It's still a long way to go. But logically, you can see: now it makes it possible. The missing component has been made.".

Recent findings suggest that from a manufacturing perspective, two of the materials used in the device, tungsten and hafnium oxide, are already widely used in semiconductor production. Graphene is newer but is actively being developed by major companies such as TSMC and Samsung, and it has already been produced at wafer scale in research environments.

The work was conducted through the CONCRETE Center, short for Center of Neuromorphic Computing under Extreme Environments, a multi-university Center of Excellence led by USC and supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research and the Air Force Research Laboratory. Key experimental work was carried out in collaboration with Dr. Sabyasachi Ganguli's team at the AFRL Materials Lab in Dayton, Ohio, while theoretical analysis involved USC researchers and collaborators at Kumamoto University in Japan.

For Yang, publication in Science reflects more than a single achievement.

"Space exploration has never been so real, so close, and at such a large scale," he said. "This paper represents a critical leap into a much larger, more exciting frontier.".

Materials provided by University of Southern California. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

There are no downloads, payments, or registration requirements to join the queue, and players can rejoin once their session ends.

Recent findings suggest that the project was created after its developers realized their PS5 spent much of its time sitting unused. Now, they’re encouraging visitors to work together to complete every GTA 6 story mission.

#161771. Latest Update: This latest chip could slash data center energy waste

📅 10 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (836 w)

Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: This latest chip could slash data center energy waste

📅 10 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (836 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As data centers consume more energy to support growing digital demands, engineers at the University of California San Diego have introduced a new chip design that could make powering graphics processing units (GPUs) more efficient.
  • The findings, published in Nature Communications, suggest the potential for smaller and more energy-efficient systems in advanced computing environments.
  • Rethinking DC-DC Converters for Modern Electronics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As data centers consume more energy to support growing digital demands, engineers at the University of California San Diego have introduced a new chip design that could make powering graphics processing units (GPUs) more efficient. The innovation focuses on a key function in electronics: converting high voltages into the lower levels required by computing hardware. In laboratory testing, a prototype chip successfully performed this type of voltage conversion with high efficiency under conditions similar to those found in modern data centers.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, suggest the potential for smaller and more energy-efficient systems in advanced computing environments.

Rethinking DC-DC Converters for Modern Electronics.

At the center of the new design is an improved version of a widely used component known as a DC-DC step-down converter. These converters are found in nearly all electronic devices and serve as a critical link between power sources and sensitive circuits. Their job is to take a high incoming voltage and reduce it to the exact level needed for safe operation.

It has been revealed that in data centers, electricity is often distributed at 48 volts, while GPU processors typically require much lower voltages, usually between 1 and 5 volts. Efficiently managing this large voltage drop has become increasingly challenging as computing systems grow more powerful and compact.

Limits of Traditional Power Conversion Technology.

Industry observers note that conventional step-down converters often struggle when dealing with large differences between input and output voltage. As that gap increases, efficiency drops and it becomes harder to supply enough current. Most existing designs rely on magnetic components such as inductors. While these components have been refined over many years, they are approaching their practical limits and are becoming harder to improve further.

"We've gotten so good at designing inductive converters that there's not really much room left to improve them to meet future needs," said study senior author Patrick Mercier, professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering.

Exploring Piezoelectric Resonators as an Alternative.

According to recent reports, to move beyond these limitations, Mercier and his team, including first author Jae-Young Ko, an electrical and computer engineering Ph.D. student at UC San Diego, investigated a different approach using piezoelectric resonators. These small devices store and transfer energy through mechanical vibrations rather than magnetic fields.

Converters based on piezoelectric components could offer several advantages. They have the potential to be smaller, more energy dense, more efficient, and easier to manufacture at scale. "They have a lot of room to grow and have the potential to deliver better performance than anything that's come before them," Mercier stated.

However, earlier versions of piezoelectric converters have had difficulty maintaining efficiency and delivering sufficient power when handling large voltage differences.

Hybrid Design Achieves High Efficiency and Power Output.

It has been revealed that to overcome these complications, the researchers created a hybrid converter that combines a piezoelectric resonator with small, commercially available capacitors arranged in a carefully designed configuration. This setup enables the system to handle larger voltage conversions more effectively.

The team incorporated this design into a prototype chip and tested its performance. The device successfully converted 48 volts down to 4.8 volts -- a level commonly required in data centers -- with a peak efficiency of 96.2 percent. It also delivered roughly four times more output current than previous piezoelectric-based designs.

This hybrid approach offers several benefits. It creates multiple pathways for energy to move through the system, reduces wasted power, and lessens the strain on the resonator. Together, these improvements enhance both efficiency and power delivery while only slightly increasing the chip's size.

Challenges and Next Steps for Real-World Use.

Although the technology shows strong promise, it is still in the early stages of development. The researchers view it as an important step toward overcoming the constraints of current power conversion systems. Future efforts will focus on refining materials, improving circuit designs, and developing better packaging methods.

Sources indicate that one challenge is that piezoelectric resonators physically vibrate, which means they cannot be attached to circuit boards using standard soldering techniques. Newly introduced integration strategies will be needed to incorporate them into electronic systems, Mercier explained.

Industry observers note that "Piezoelectric-based converters aren't quite ready to replace existing power converter technologies yet," Mercier added. "But they offer a trajectory for improvement. We need to continue to improve on multiple areas -- materials, circuits and packaging -- to make this technology ready for data center applications.".

This project was supported in part by the Power Management Integration Center (PMIC), an Industry-University Cooperative Research Center (IUCRC) funded by the National Science Foundation (award number 2052809).

McSorley remained outside until the woman’s cries became clearer, allowing him to hear her asking for help after suffering a fall. He immediately called 911 and waited for emergency services to arrive.

First responders transported the woman to a nearby hospital. According to Carver EMS, she had been lying on the floor for approximately 45 minutes without access to a phone or a medical alert device.

Carver EMS Chief Michael Ryan credited the delivery driver’s actions with preventing the woman from potentially spending much longer on the floor.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Animal rights organization PETA is urging Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to ditch his iconic black leather jacket, even sending the billionaire an $875 vegan alternative made from olive waste.

Much like Steve Jobs with his black turtlenecks and Mark Zuckerberg with his gray T-shirts, Huang’s leather jackets have become synonymous with the Nvidia boss.

His signature look has even proven lucrative. In July 2026, one of Huang’s signed Tom Ford leather jackets sold for a staggering $960,000 at auction, fetching 16 times its estimated price.

However, following Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO amid an ongoing foreign intelligence investigation for cheating on his wife with an alleged Chinese spy, PETA wants the billionaire to give his wardrobe an upgrade.

In a November 18 letter addressed to Huang, PETA President Tracy Reiman argued that despite his reputation as a technological innovator, his fashion choices were outdated.

“Tech doesn’t move forward by clinging to outdated systems, and neither does fashion,” Reiman stated. “PETA is calling on everyone to embrace vegan leathers made from cactus, cork, apples, and other plant materials and leave animals out of their wardrobes.”.

To encourage Huang to make the switch, PETA sent him an $875 jacket from fashion brand Benedetti Life, according to the Fresh York Post.

The jacket is made using Oleatex, a leather alternative derived from olive harvesting waste. It features an organic cotton lining and an exterior consisting of 95% Biotex and 5% polyurethane.

PETA has also asked Huang to donate his old leather jacket to its planned Museum of Animal-Sourced Atrocities, offering the billionaire the prospect of a tax deduction in return.

Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO amid ongoing foreign intelligence investigation.

Interestingly, Huang had already ditched his trademark look when he returned to Nvidia’s headquarters on November 23. However, rather than opting for PETA’s olive-based alternative, he appeared to be sporting a $3,300 Dior cotton jacket, according to GQ.

In a recent development, whether Huang is willing to part ways with his extensive leather jacket collection remains to be seen. The Nvidia boss previously revealed that he owns between 30 and 40 of them.

“Giant superatoms” could finally solve quantum computing’s biggest problem

📅 13 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have introduced a new theoretical design for quantum systems based on what they call "giant superatoms." This concept offers a fresh way to protect, control, and share quantum information, potentially bringing scientists closer to building large-scale quantum computers.
  • Recent findings suggest that quantum computers are expected to transform fields like drug discovery and encryption by solving problems that are far beyond the reach of conventional machines.
  • "Quantum systems are extraordinarily powerful but also extremely fragile.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have introduced a new theoretical design for quantum systems based on what they call "giant superatoms." This concept offers a fresh way to protect, control, and share quantum information, potentially bringing scientists closer to building large-scale quantum computers.

Recent findings suggest that quantum computers are expected to transform fields like drug discovery and encryption by solving problems that are far beyond the reach of conventional machines. However, progress has been limited by a major challenge known as decoherence. This occurs when quantum bits, or qubits, lose their information due to interactions with their surroundings. Even small amounts of electromagnetic noise can disrupt the fragile quantum states needed for computation.

"Quantum systems are extraordinarily powerful but also extremely fragile. The key to making them useful is learning how to control their interaction with the surrounding environment," indicates Lei Du, postdoctoral researcher in applied quantum technology at Chalmers.

It has been revealed that lei Du is the lead author of a study that outlines this latest type of quantum system. The design is built around giant superatoms, which combine several important features. These systems reduce decoherence, remain stable, and consist of multiple interconnected "atoms" that function together as a single unit.

Giant superatoms bring together two previously separate ideas in quantum physics: giant atoms and superatoms. While each has been studied on its own, this is the first time they have been merged into a single system. These structures behave like atoms but are not found in nature. Instead, they are engineered by scientists (see fact box below).

Giant Atoms and Their "Quantum Echo".

The idea of giant atoms was first introduced by researchers at Chalmers over a decade ago and is now widely used in the field. A giant atom is typically designed as a qubit (which is the smallest unit of quantum information). Unlike ordinary atoms, it connects to light or sound waves at multiple, physically separated points. This allows it to interact with its environment in several places at once, helping it preserve quantum information.

"Waves that leave one connection point can travel through the environment and return to affect the atom at another point -- similar to hearing an echo of your own voice before you've finished speaking. This self-interaction leads to highly beneficial quantum effects, reduces decoherence and gives the system a form of memory of past interactions," explains Anton Frisk Kockum, Associate Professor of Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Extending Entanglement Across Distances.

Although giant atoms have improved understanding of quantum behavior, they have had limitations when it comes to entanglement. Entanglement allows multiple qubits to share a single quantum state and act as one coordinated system, which is essential for powerful quantum computers.

To overcome this limitation, the research team combined giant atoms with the concept of superatoms. A superatom consists of several natural atoms that share the same quantum state and behave collectively as one larger atom.

This combination is expected to make it easier to create complex quantum states needed for quantum communication, networks, and highly sensitive measurement systems.

"A giant superatom may be envisaged as multiple giant atoms working together as a single entity, exhibiting a non-local interaction between light and matter. This enables quantum information from multiple qubits to be stored and controlled within one unit, without the need for increasingly complex surrounding circuitry," explains Lei Du.

Sources indicate that "Giant superatoms open the door to entirely upcoming capabilities, giving us a powerful new toolbox. They allow us to control quantum information and create entanglement in ways that were previously extremely difficult, or even impossible," says Janine Splettstoesser, Professor of Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Toward Scalable and Practical Quantum Systems.

This work creates new possibilities for building quantum systems that are both scalable and reliable. The researchers plan to move from theory toward actually constructing these systems. Their design could also be integrated with other quantum technologies, serving as a building block for connecting different types of quantum platforms.

In a recent development, "There is right now strong interest in hybrid approaches, in which different quantum systems work together, because each has its own strengths," notes Anton Frisk Kockum. "Our research demonstrates that smart design can reduce the need for increasingly complex hardware and giant superatoms are bringing us one step closer to practically applicable quantum technology.".

Controlling Quantum Information Flow.

More on: Methods for protecting, controlling and distributing quantum information.

It has been revealed that the study shows that the way giant superatoms interact with light depends on their internal quantum states. This discovery gives researchers greater control over how quantum information moves through a system. They describe two different ways of connecting these structures to achieve useful outcomes.

In one setup, several giant superatoms are closely linked in a specific arrangement. This allows them to pass quantum states between each other without decoherence, meaning no information is lost.

In another setup, the atoms are spaced farther apart but connected in a carefully tuned way so that waves remain synchronized. This makes it possible to direct quantum signals and distribute entanglement over long distances.

Understanding Giant Atoms and Superatoms.

Superatoms and giant atoms are engineered systems that behave like atoms rather than naturally occurring ones.

A superatom is a quantum system made up of multiple natural atoms that share a single quantum state and respond to light as one entity.

A giant atom, on the other hand, connects to light or sound waves at several separate points in space. It is called "giant" because it is larger than the wavelength of the light it interacts with.

Giant atoms have defined energy levels and follow the rules of quantum mechanics, yet they can reach sizes of up to millimeters, making them visible to the naked eye. Through electromagnetic or acoustic waves, they can interact with their surroundings at multiple locations at the same time. One way to picture this is as a single atom linked to a wave at several distant points. This unusual setup allows the atom to be influenced by the waves it produces.

Breaking: This simple change stops robot swarms from getting stuck

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine a swarm of robots rushing to complete an urgent job, such as cleaning up an oil spill or assembling complex machinery.
  • This raises a simple but important question: in a limited area, how many robots can you deploy before efficiency starts to drop?
  • According to recent reports, A fresh study from the lab of L.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine a swarm of robots rushing to complete an urgent job, such as cleaning up an oil spill or assembling complex machinery. At first, adding more robots speeds things up. But after a certain point, the space becomes crowded, robots start interfering with one another, and overall progress slows.

This raises a simple but important question: in a limited area, how many robots can you deploy before efficiency starts to drop? Researchers at Harvard believe they have found a clear answer.

A Simple Idea That Boosts Efficiency.

According to recent reports, A fresh study from the lab of L. Mahadevan, the Lola England de Valpine Professor of Applied Mathematics, Organismic and Evolutionary Biology, and Physics, reveals that adding a controlled amount of randomness to how robots move can reduce congestion and improve performance in crowded environments.

Sources indicate that the work combines mathematical modeling, computer simulations, and real-world experiments. It demonstrates how basic local movement rules can lead to organized, efficient outcomes on a larger scale. The findings could influence how robotic fleets are designed and may even apply to human crowd management and traffic flow. The research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and led by applied mathematics Ph.D. student Lucy Liu, with guidance from SEAS Senior Research Fellow Justin Werfel.

Why Randomness Helps Predict Complex Behavior.

Studying dense crowds is difficult because individuals can take countless possible paths and interact in unpredictable ways, Liu explained. To simplify the problem, the researchers treated each robot as a basic unit with a small, adjustable amount of variation in its movement.

In a recent development, "This might be counterintuitive, because how could randomness make things easier to work with?" stated Liu. "But in this case, when you have a lot of randomness, it becomes possible to take averages -- average distances, average times, average behaviors. This makes it a lot easier to make predictions.".

Simulating Robot Swarms in Motion.

Recent findings suggest that to explore this idea, the team created computer simulations of robot groups, referred to as agents. Each agent started at a random location and was assigned a random destination. Once it reached its target, it immediately received a new one, mimicking continuous task assignment in real-world systems.

Recent findings suggest that each agent moved toward its goal with a tunable amount of variation, described as "noise." With no noise, agents moved in straight lines. With high noise, their paths became erratic and inefficient. However, this wandering also helped them navigate around one another.

Finding the "Goldilocks Zone" of Noise.

Industry observers note that the simulations revealed a clear pattern. When agents moved in perfectly straight paths, they quickly formed dense clusters and traffic jams that halted progress. When movement became too random, congestion disappeared but efficiency dropped due to excessive wandering.

Between these extremes, the researchers identified a sweet spot. In this range, agents occasionally bumped into one another and formed short-lived clusters, but still managed to slip past and keep moving. This balance allowed the system to maintain a steady flow.

From Simulations to Mathematical Models.

In a recent development, using these insights, the team developed formulas to estimate "goal attainment rate," or how many destinations are reached over time. These equations made it possible to determine the ideal combination of crowd density and movement randomness to maximize performance.

Testing the Theory With Real Robots.

To confirm their findings, Liu collaborated with physicist Federico Toschi at Eindhoven University of Technology in the Netherlands. Together, they set up experiments with small wheeled robots in a lab equipped with an overhead camera.

Each robot carried a QR code so its position could be tracked and updated with upcoming destinations. Although the physical robots moved more slowly and less precisely than the simulated agents, they displayed the same overall patterns.

It has been revealed that the experiments supported a key idea: highly complex coordination does not require advanced intelligence or centralized control. Instead, simple local rules can produce effective group behavior, at least within certain density limits.

"Understanding how active matter, whether it is a swarm of ants, a herd of animals, or a group of robots, become functional and execute tasks in crowded environments using the principles of self-organization, is relevant to many questions in behavioral ecology," Mahadevan said. "Our study suggests strategies that might well be much broader than the instantiation we have focused on.".

Recent findings suggest that liu noted that she has long been interested in designing safer and more efficient crowded spaces. This research points toward a future where the movement of large groups, whether robots, vehicles, or people, could be predicted and optimized using mathematical tools.

The results suggest that introducing controlled variability into movement patterns may improve flow in many real-world systems, from factory floors to city streets.

Funding for the research came from the National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship Program under Grant No. DGE 2140743, along with grants from the Simons Foundation and the Henri Seydoux Fund.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 103-year-old gaming grandmother is taking part in a Tekken tournament, with one of her closest rivals also being 95 years old.

It has been revealed that even though gaming, and especially esports, are seen as a hobby for the younger generation, there are plenty of older folks who get involved as well. Those who grew up on the likes of the PlayStation One, Atari 2600, NES, and even the Sega Genesis still want to be involved.

Over in Japan, the Care Esports Association runs competitive gaming events aimed at senior citizens throughout the year, with an annual event taking place in December around Tekken 8.

Typically, competitors are aged between 70 and 90, but this year, they’ve cracked the 100-year-old mark, with a 103-year-old grandmother taking part.

As per Denfaminico, 103-year-old Toshiko Morishita will play in this year’s event, which is also looking to set a Guinness World Record for the “highest average age of esports tournament participants.”.

According to the outlet, the 103-year-old knows that her age might be a barrier to success, but said that even losing would still be “enjoyable” for her.

She “enjoys the game” without “being solely focused on winning or losing,” but has been putting in practice to prepare for the event.

As noted, competitors at the event typically range from 70 to 90 years old, with last year’s winner – Hisako Sakai – clocking in at 92 years old.

Sakai fought her way to first place using Claudio Serafino and defeated 95-year-old Sadayuki Kato in the semifinals.

The average age at last year’s event was just under 87, so having a 103-year-old competing will drag that up – hopefully, for them, into Guinness World Records territory.

Quantum AI just got shockingly good at predicting chaos

📅 18 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fresh study led by researchers at UCL (University College London) shows that combining quantum computing with artificial intelligence can significantly improve predictions of complex physical systems over long periods.
  • In a recent development, the results, published in Science Advances, could enhance simulations of how liquids and gases behave, known as fluid dynamics.
  • In a recent development, the improved accuracy appears to come from how quantum computers process information.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fresh study led by researchers at UCL (University College London) shows that combining quantum computing with artificial intelligence can significantly improve predictions of complex physical systems over long periods. The hybrid approach outperforms leading models that rely only on conventional computers.

In a recent development, the results, published in Science Advances, could enhance simulations of how liquids and gases behave, known as fluid dynamics. These types of models are essential in fields such as climate science, transportation, medicine, and energy production.

Why Quantum Computing Makes a Difference.

In a recent development, the improved accuracy appears to come from how quantum computers process information. Unlike traditional computers that use bits set to either 1 or 0, quantum computers use qubits, which can exist as 1, 0, or anything in between. In addition, each qubit can influence others, allowing a relatively small number of qubits to represent an enormous number of possible states.

Professor Peter Coveney, senior author from UCL Chemistry and the Advanced Research Computing Centre, explained the challenge: "To make predictions about complex systems, we can either run a full simulation, which might take weeks -- often too long to be useful -- or we can use an AI model which is quicker but more unreliable over longer time scales.

"Our quantum-informed AI model means we could provide more accurate predictions quickly. Making predictions about fluid flow and turbulence is a fundamental science challenge but it also has many applications. Our method can be used in climate forecasting, in modeling blood flow and the interaction of molecules, or to better design wind farms so they generate more energy.".

How the Hybrid Quantum-AI Method Works.

Although quantum computers are widely expected to surpass classical machines in power, their real-world use has so far been limited. This new approach integrates quantum computing into a specific stage of the AI training process.

Industry observers note that typically, AI models learn from large datasets generated by simulations or observations. In this case, the data is first processed by a quantum computer, which identifies key statistical patterns that remain stable over time. These patterns, known as invariant statistical properties, are then used to guide the training of an AI model running on a conventional supercomputer.

Higher Accuracy With Less Memory.

The quantum-informed AI system delivered about 20 percent greater accuracy compared to standard AI models that did not use quantum-derived patterns. It also maintained stable predictions over longer periods, even when modeling chaotic systems.

Recent findings suggest that another major advantage was efficiency. The method required hundreds of times less memory, making it far more practical for large-scale simulations.

Quantum Effects Behind the Efficiency.

This performance boost comes from two defining features of quantum computing. Entanglement allows qubits to influence each other regardless of distance, while superposition enables a qubit to exist in multiple states at once until measured. Together, these properties allow quantum systems to process vast amounts of information in a compact form.

Demonstrating Practical Quantum Advantage.

First author Maida Wang of the UCL Centre for Computational Science said: "Our fresh method appears to demonstrate 'quantum advantage' in a practical way -- that is, the quantum computer outperforms what is possible through classical computing alone. These findings could inspire the development of novel classical approaches that achieve even higher accuracy, though they would likely lack the remarkable data compression and parameter efficiency offered by our method. The next steps are to scale up the method using larger datasets and to apply it to real-world situations which typically involve even more complexity. In addition, a provable theoretical framework will be proposed.".

Co-first author Xiao Xue, from Advanced Research Computing at UCL, added: "In this work, we demonstrate for the first time that quantum computing can be meaningfully integrated with classical machine learning methods to tackle complex dynamical systems, including fluid mechanics. It is exciting to see this kind of 'quantum-informed' approach moving towards practical use.".

Capturing the Physics of Complex Systems.

The researchers suggest that quantum computers are particularly well suited to modeling these systems because they can compactly represent their underlying physics. Many complex systems behave in ways that resemble quantum effects, where changes in one region can influence distant parts of the system, similar to entanglement.

Overcoming Limits of Current Quantum Hardware.

Industry observers note that current quantum computers face challenges such as noise, errors, and interference, which often require large numbers of measurements. The newly introduced method avoids these challenges by using the quantum computer only once during the workflow, rather than repeatedly exchanging data between quantum and classical systems.

Experiment Details and Future Potential.

The study used a 20-qubit IQM quantum computer connected to powerful classical computing resources at the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Germany.

To function, quantum computers must operate at extremely low temperatures, around minus 273C (close to absolute zero, colder than anything in space).

The research was funded by UCL and the UK's Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC), with additional support from IQM Quantum Computers and the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich.

As researchers continue to scale up this approach, it could open the door to more accurate and efficient predictions across a wide range of scientific and engineering applications.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japan is expanding its AI crackdown on manga and anime piracy overseas after testing a system that can find websites hosting unauthorized copies.

Recent findings suggest that on November 24, The Yomiuri Shimbun reported that Japan’s Agency for Cultural Affairs found pirated manga on 94% of the 1,935 websites its AI flagged for suspected manga piracy. Of the 1,564 sites flagged for suspected anime piracy, 89% hosted unauthorized copies.

For its overseas tests, the agency trained the AI to recognize domain names commonly associated with piracy sites and could compile the results as early as March 2027.

Japan’s latest anti-piracy push follows an April 3 discussion in the country’s House of Representatives, where executives from some of Japan’s biggest animation studios warned that piracy remains one of the biggest obstacles to anime’s growth overseas.

Among them was Toei Animation, the studio behind One Piece and Dragon Ball, which called for stronger government action on anime piracy.

According to data published by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry, piracy losses from digital content rose from two trillion yen in 2022 to 5.7 trillion yen in 2025, increasing from roughly $13.3 billion to around $38 billion USD.

In a bid to curb those losses, Japan’s Agency for Cultural Affairs has also expanded its AI piracy tests to target overseas sites hosting unauthorized copies of manga and anime, with looks to compile its findings as early as March 2027.

#161762. Latest Update: Think AI "knows" what it’s doing? Scientists say think again

📅 19 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1095 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Think AI "knows" what it’s doing? Scientists say think again

📅 19 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1095 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These are everyday words people use to describe what goes on in the human mind.
  • Sources indicate that "We use mental verbs all the time in our daily lives, so it makes sense that we might also use them when we talk about machines -- it helps us relate to them," noted Jo Mackiewicz, professor of English at Iowa State.
  • Mackiewicz and Jeanine Aune, a teaching professor of English and director of the advanced communication program at Iowa State, are part of a research team that studied how writers describe AI using human-like language.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Think, know, understand, remember.

These are everyday words people use to describe what goes on in the human mind. But when those same terms are applied to artificial intelligence, they can unintentionally make machines seem more human than they really are.

Sources indicate that "We use mental verbs all the time in our daily lives, so it makes sense that we might also use them when we talk about machines -- it helps us relate to them," noted Jo Mackiewicz, professor of English at Iowa State. "But at the same time, when we apply mental verbs to machines, there's also a risk of blurring the line between what humans and AI can do.".

Mackiewicz and Jeanine Aune, a teaching professor of English and director of the advanced communication program at Iowa State, are part of a research team that studied how writers describe AI using human-like language. This type of wording, known as anthropomorphism, assigns human traits to non-human systems. Their study, "Anthropomorphizing Artificial Intelligence: A Corpus Study of Mental Verbs Used with AI and ChatGPT," was published in Technical Communication Quarterly.

It has been revealed that the research team also included Matthew J. Baker, associate professor of linguistics at Brigham Young University, and Jordan Smith, assistant professor of English at the University of Northern Colorado. Both previously studied at Iowa State University.

Why Human-Like Language About AI Can Be Misleading.

According to recent reports, according to the researchers, using mental verbs to describe AI can create a false impression. Words such as "think," "know," "understand," and "want" suggest that a system has thoughts, intentions, or awareness. In reality, AI does not possess beliefs or feelings. It produces responses by analyzing patterns in data, not by forming ideas or making conscious decisions.

Mackiewicz and Aune also pointed out that this kind of language can overstate what AI is capable of. Phrases like "AI decided" or "ChatGPT knows" can make systems seem more independent or intelligent than they actually are. This can lead to unrealistic expectations about how reliable or capable AI is.

It has been revealed that there is also a broader concern. When AI is described as if it has intentions, it can distract from the humans behind it. Developers, engineers, and organizations are responsible for how these systems are built and used.

"Certain anthropomorphic phrases may even stick in readers' minds and can potentially shape public perception of AI in unhelpful ways," Aune mentioned.

How News Writers Actually Use AI Language.

To better understand how often this kind of language appears, the researchers analyzed the News on the Web (NOW) corpus. This massive dataset contains more than 20 billion words from English-language news articles published in 20 countries.

They focused on how frequently mental verbs such as "learns," "means," and "knows" were used alongside terms like AI and ChatGPT.

Mental Verbs Are Less Common Than Expected.

The study found that news writers do not frequently pair AI-related terms with mental verbs.

Recent findings suggest that while anthropomorphism is common in everyday speech, it appears far less often in news writing. "Anthropomorphism has been shown to be common in everyday speech, but we found there's far less usage in news writing," Mackiewicz said.

Among the examples identified, the word "needs" appeared most often with AI, showing up 661 times. For ChatGPT, "knows" was the most frequent pairing, but it appeared only 32 times.

The researchers noted that editorial standards may play a role. Associated Press guidelines, which discourage attributing human emotions or traits to AI, could be influencing how journalists write about these technologies.

Context Matters More Than the Words Themselves.

Even when mental verbs were used, they were not always anthropomorphic.

In a recent development, for instance, the word "needs" often described basic requirements rather than human-like qualities. Phrases such as "AI needs large amounts of data" or "AI needs some human assistance" are similar to how people describe non-human systems like cars or recipes. In these cases, the language does not imply that AI has thoughts or desires.

In other cases, "needs" was used to express what should be done, such as "AI needs to be trained" or "AI needs to be implemented." Aune explained that these examples were often written in passive voice, which shifts responsibility back to human actors rather than the technology itself.

Anthropomorphism Exists on a Spectrum.

It has been revealed that the study also indicated that not all uses of mental verbs are equal. Some phrases move closer to suggesting human-like qualities.

For example, statements like "AI needs to understand the real world" can imply expectations tied to human reasoning, ethics, or awareness. These uses go beyond simple descriptions and begin to suggest deeper capabilities.

"These instances showed that anthropomorphizing isn't all-or-nothing and instead exists on a spectrum," Aune stated.

Why Language Choices About AI Matter.

Overall, the researchers found that anthropomorphism in news coverage is both less frequent and more nuanced than many might assume.

Industry observers note that "Overall, our analysis indicates that anthropomorphization of AI in news writing is far less common -- and far more nuanced -- than we might think," Mackiewicz noted. "Even the instances that did anthropomorphize AI varied widely in strength.".

Recent findings suggest that the findings highlight the importance of context. Simply counting words is not enough to understand how language shapes meaning.

"For writers, this nuance matters: the language we choose shapes how readers understand AI systems, their capabilities and the humans responsible for them," Mackiewicz noted.

The research team also emphasized that these insights can help professionals think more carefully about how they describe AI in their work.

"Our findings can help technical and professional communication practitioners reflect on how they think about AI technologies as tools in their writing process and how they write about AI," the research team wrote in the published study.

Sources indicate that as AI continues to develop, the way people talk about it will remain important. Mackiewicz and Aune said writers will need to stay mindful of how word choices influence perception.

Looking ahead, the team suggested that future studies could explore how different words shape understanding and whether even rare uses of anthropomorphic language have a strong impact on how people view AI.

Materials provided by Iowa State University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Over the first three days of the launch week, though, worldwide workouts dropped by 10% compared to the weeks before.

“Our data suggests that for three days, many people chose to work out in Vice City rather than in the gym,” noted Yossi Tarablus, VP of Marketing, Fitness22.

It wasn’t just workouts and gym numbers that were impacted by the launch. An estimated 1.5 million people in the United States took at least one day off to play GTA 6. That was said to cost the economy around $1 billion.

Unlike in GTA, there is no real cheat code to bulk up in real life other than putting in the hard work.

#161760. Tech Report: Artificial neurons successfully communicate with living brain cells

📅 18 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1158 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Artificial neurons successfully communicate with living brain cells

📅 18 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1158 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Engineers at Northwestern University have created printed artificial neurons that go beyond imitation and can directly interact with real brain cells.
  • In experiments using slices of mouse brain, the artificial neurons successfully triggered responses in real neurons.
  • According to recent reports, this advance moves researchers closer to electronics that can directly interface with the nervous system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Engineers at Northwestern University have created printed artificial neurons that go beyond imitation and can directly interact with real brain cells. These flexible, low-cost devices produce electrical signals that closely resemble those generated by living neurons, allowing them to activate biological brain tissue.

In experiments using slices of mouse brain, the artificial neurons successfully triggered responses in real neurons. This result shows a latest level of compatibility between electronic devices and living neural systems.

Toward Brain Interfaces and Energy-Efficient AI.

According to recent reports, this advance moves researchers closer to electronics that can directly interface with the nervous system. Potential uses include brain-machine interfaces and neuroprosthetics, such as implants that could help restore hearing, vision, or movement.

According to recent reports, the technology also points toward a latest generation of computing systems inspired by the brain. By replicating how neurons communicate, future hardware could perform complex tasks using far less energy. The brain remains the most energy-efficient computing system known, and scientists hope to apply its principles to modern technology.

The study will be published on April 15 in the journal Nature Nanotechnology.

"The world we live in today is dominated by artificial intelligence (AI)," mentioned Northwestern's Mark C. Hersam, who led the study. "The way you make AI smarter is by training it on more and more data. This data-intensive training leads to a massive power-consumption problem. Therefore, we have to come up with more efficient hardware to handle substantial data and AI. Because the brain is five orders of magnitude more energy efficient than a digital computer, it makes sense to look to the brain for inspiration for next-generation computing.".

Hersam is an expert in brain-inspired computing and holds multiple roles at Northwestern University, including the Walter P. Murphy Professor of Materials Science and Engineering at the McCormick School of Engineering. He also is a professor of medicine at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine and a professor of chemistry at the Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences. In addition, he serves as chair of the department of materials science and engineering, director of the Materials Research Science and Engineering Center, and a member of the International Institute for Nanotechnology. He co-led the study with Vinod K. Sangwan, a research associate professor at McCormick.

Why the Brain Outperforms Traditional Silicon.

Modern computers handle increasing workloads by packing billions of identical transistors onto rigid, two-dimensional silicon chips. Each component behaves the same way, and once manufactured, the system remains fixed.

Recent findings suggest that the brain works very differently. It consists of many types of neurons, each with specialized roles, arranged in soft, three-dimensional networks. These networks are constantly changing, forming and adjusting connections as learning occurs.

"Silicon achieves complexity by having billions of identical devices," Hersam said. "Everything is the same, rigid and fixed once it's fabricated. The brain is the opposite. It's heterogeneous, dynamic and three-dimensional. To move in that direction, we need latest materials and new ways to build electronics.".

Although artificial neurons have been developed before, most produce overly simple signals. To achieve more complex behavior, engineers typically need large networks of devices, which increases energy use.

Printable Materials Enable Brain-Like Behavior.

Industry observers note that to better replicate real neural activity, Hersam's team built artificial neurons using soft, printable materials that more closely match the brain's structure. Their approach relies on electronic inks made from nanoscale flakes of molybdenum disulfide (MoS2), which acts as a semiconductor, and graphene, which serves as an electrical conductor. These materials were deposited onto flexible polymer surfaces using aerosol jet printing.

Previously, researchers treated the polymer in these inks as a flaw because it interfered with electrical performance. As a result, they removed it after printing. In this work, the team used that same feature to enhance the device.

Industry observers note that "Instead of fully removing the polymer, we partially decompose it," he said. "Then, when we pass current through the device, we drive further decomposition of the polymer. This decomposition occurs in a spatially inhomogeneous manner, leading to formation of a conductive filament, such that all the current is constricted into a narrow region in space.".

That narrow conductive path produces a sudden electrical response similar to a neuron firing. The resulting device can generate a wide variety of signals, including single spikes, continuous firing, and bursting patterns, closely resembling real neural communication.

Because each artificial neuron can produce more complex signals, fewer components are needed to perform advanced tasks. This could significantly improve computing efficiency.

Testing Artificial Neurons on Real Brain Tissue.

To evaluate whether the artificial neurons could truly interact with living systems, the researchers partnered with Indira M. Raman, the Bill and Gayle Cook Professor of Neurobiology at Weinberg. Her team applied the artificial signals to slices of mouse cerebellum.

The results showed that the electrical spikes matched key biological properties, including their timing and duration. These signals reliably activated real neurons and triggered neural circuits in a way similar to natural brain activity.

It has been revealed that "Other labs have tried to make artificial neurons with organic materials, and they spiked too slowly," Hersam noted. "Or they used metal oxides, which are too fast. We are within a temporal range that was not previously demonstrated for artificial neurons. You can see the living neurons respond to our artificial neuron. So, we've demonstrated signals that are not only the right timescale but also the right spike shape to interact directly with living neurons.".

Low-Cost, Sustainable Manufacturing and AI Implications.

Beyond performance, the new approach offers environmental and practical advantages. The manufacturing process is simple and inexpensive, and the additive printing method places material only where it is needed, reducing waste.

In a recent development, improving energy efficiency is especially crucial as artificial intelligence systems grow more demanding. Large data centers already consume vast amounts of power and require significant water for cooling.

"To meet the energy demands of AI, tech companies are building gigawatt data centers powered by dedicated nuclear power plants," Hersam remarked. "It is evident that this massive power consumption will limit further scaling of computing since it's hard to imagine a next-generation data center requiring 100 nuclear power plants. The other issue is that when you're dissipating gigawatts of power, there's a lot of heat. Because data centers are cooled with water, AI is putting severe stress on the water supply. However you look at it, we need to come up with more energy-efficient hardware for AI.".

The study, "Multi-order complexity spiking neurons enabled by printed MoS2 memristive nanosheet networks," was supported by the National Science Foundation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI data centers in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, and Indonesia are facing trouble as Nvidia has reportedly ordered its manufacturing partners to stop shipping AI servers to the region. According to the Financial Times, Dell, Supermicro, and other firms that make AI servers using Nvidia AI GPUs have told their customers from the four countries that the AI chip maker has forbidden them to ship their orders. The move comes as the U.S. closed the loophole that let Chinese AI companies rent compute from data centers outside China equipped with advanced AI chips sourced from American semiconductor manufacturers like Nvidia.

Sources indicate that the U.S. has banned the export of advanced AI chips to China since 2022 in an effort to limit its advancement. Even though President Trump eventually allowed Nvidia to export H100 AI GPUs to China in December 2025, companies that wanted to buy them needed to secure an import license from the Commerce Department. Aside from that, the White House is also collecting a 25% fee for every chip, making it more expensive for a data center in China to buy them. Because of this, many Chinese AI labs are instead renting compute from data centers located abroad. They mostly do this in Southeast Asia, which is just around a four-to-six-hour flight from major cities like Hong Kong, Shenzhen, and Shanghai, although some firms are looking in further areas like Europe.

It has been revealed that it remains unclear if Nvidia’s order is permanent or temporary, but the newly introduced export rules give cloud providers 90 days to apply for an export license and prove that their customers do not include restricted entities. However, one cloud provider executive told the Financial Times that there are no clear instructions on how to go about this. “There’s this new rule but no guidance on execution,” they remarked. “No one knows how to apply for this license while the 90-day clock is ticking. It’s causing sheer chaos in the region.”.

Sources indicate that this sudden halt of orders is causing trouble for many data centers in Southeast Asia. Sources say that Aolani, a Singapore-based cloud company with a deal to provide compute to ByteDance, is losing financing for the project as bankers have stopped issuing credit to the tune of $500 million as Nvidia GPU shipments to the region remain in jeopardy. The Chinese social media giant could also potentially drop out of the arrangement, as it won’t be able to access the powerful Nvidia chips that many AI labs still prefer for training their models.
