📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This reveals that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors.".

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors.

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

According to recent reports, to counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%.

According to recent reports, the researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

Sources indicate that when the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Recent findings suggest that although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the fresh technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error.".

A Fresh Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors.

Recent findings suggest that the findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

According to recent reports, this is especially crucial for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," claims Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations.".

Industry observers note that the broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

📅 26 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a fresh generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity.
  • Industry observers note that A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them.
  • Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a fresh generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an key role in how computers store and process data.

Industry observers note that A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers.

Recent findings suggest that the potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also crucial to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," stated Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an notable advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time.

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

According to recent reports, in the upcoming study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

Recent findings suggest that "For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A Latest Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing.

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly vital if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a fresh way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us latest insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become vital for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," remarked Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

And when people are brought together, there’s always alcohol on the table.” Read, who says she was never much of a drinker to begin with, started limiting her consumption to a drink or two at work-related events about five years ago. I have to be up early in the morning, and it was starting to affect my sleep,” she says. “It just had downstream impacts that I really wasn’t appreciating.” Read says her colleagues supported her decision to give up alcohol completely, but says it’s still hard to navigate professional situations with newly introduced people, like networking events. “I had trepidation about being fully sober because I knew it was an awkward conversation to have,” she says. “Sometimes I will hold a glass of sparkling water instead of champagne to not feel like I need to explain myself.” Read isn’t the only one who occasionally finds strategies to avoid conversations about her sobriety. According to a recent survey by the Boca Recovery Center, which operates addiction treatment centers in Florida, Indiana, Massachusetts, and New Jersey, 39% of Americans who abstain from alcohol hide their sobriety at work and 30% fake it to blend in—like drinking sparkling water from a champagne flute. And 13% have skipped a work event, celebration, or date to avoid the topic altogether. Given that more than half of sober Americans have been questioned, pressured, or teased about their decision not to consume alcohol, according to the survey, it is perhaps no surprise that 58% hide it from at least some people in their lives, and that 13% haven’t told anyone. “The holidays make this harder, as events tend to be based around drinking,” says Alison Tarlow, a licensed clinical psychologist who is the chief clinical officer at Boca Recovery Center. “Those hiding their sobriety are managing a drink, an excuse and a conversation all at once—which is socially exhausting in a setting that is supposed to be fun and relaxed.” Stigma remains even as more Americans go sober More Americans are choosing to go alcohol-free for a wide variety of reasons, though taboos related to addiction and mental health remain. According to the survey, one in four Americans have experimented with alcohol-free or reduced-drinking challenges; half of these cite physical or mental health-related reasons, compared with 10% who were recovering from addiction. Against this backdrop, younger generations appear less likely than others to hide their sobriety. According to the survey, only 5% of Gen Z keep it a secret, compared with 12% of millennials and 20% of Gen Xers. But these younger Americans also face the most outside stigma, as 68% of sober Gen Zs have faced questioning, pressure, or teasing compared with 49% of older sober Americans. “Telling people tends to involve fielding questions, which is generally off-putting to those who made such a personal decision,” says Tarlow. “Sobriety is a complex and sensitive decision, and people want to choose who hears about it and when.” Navigating the holiday party season without alcohol The holidays can be an especially challenging time for those who are looking to stay sober. Between personal and professional events, family and financial obligations ramping up, and work responsibilities starting to dwindle, many are left without some of the support systems, practical reasons, or reminders that help them maintain sobriety. Though they may feel judged for ordering an alcohol-free alternative, 93% of Americans say they would not think less of a coworker who skips alcohol at a work event, according to the survey. “The judgment sober people anticipate is usually harsher than what their peers tend to think,” says Tarlow. While colleagues may ask questions, she emphasizes that those who choose sobriety don’t need to explain themselves. “’I’m not drinking tonight’ is perfectly fine,” Tarlow says. “These events are meant to be fun, so focus on enjoying yourself, not others’ expectations. But, if pressure builds, there’s no shame in taking a break or leaving.” Coming up with excuses for not drinking can be exhausting and dishonest, says Phillip Barbb, an executive coach who specializes in sobriety. “You don’t want to feel like you have to have 25 conversations where you’re lying at the holiday party,” he says. “Creating this false narrative for yourself can weigh on you, because you’re building a gap between yourself and others.” Instead, Barbb, who has been sober for almost 19 years himself, suggests preparing a short explanation in advance that feels authentic and genuine, like, “I’m doing it for health reasons,” or “I decided I wanted to try not drinking this holiday season.” Some may also find it helpful to create a practical reason for staying sober to help them through workplace holiday events, like being a designated driver or making an early-morning commitment for the following day. Those trying to stick to their sobriety goals can also enlist the support of a colleague, date, or friend, though Barbb warns that these people shouldn’t be made responsible for someone else’s choices. “It is no one else’s responsibility to keep me sober or to keep me out of bad situations,” he says. “What I do think is cool is saying, ‘I want to go to the event, I don’t want to drink, so I may have a moment or two where I need to pull you aside to just talk or vent.’” How employers can offer more inclusive holiday parties for sober staff With so many Americans experimenting with sobriety—and so many hiding it from their colleagues—organizations will inevitably strategy holiday parties for attendees who are abstaining from alcohol, whether the organization knows it or not. So it’s important for employers to consider ways they can make the environment more inclusive for workers who don’t want to drink. When a holiday party’s primary activity is consumption, it can make those who are going sober stand out. That is why employers are encouraged to include other activities, like bowling, an escape room, or mini golf. Choice of venue can also play a role, as an event held at a bar or club may create more anxiety—and discourage more from attending—than one held at an activity venue or restaurant. “If you’re hosting an event, you do have a responsibility to offer more than just beer and wine so that people can feel comfortable,” Barbb adds. “If you’re offering signature drinks, do a version without alcohol.” Workplace cultures are often set at the top, meaning it’s up to leaders to model responsible behavior and signal inclusivity for sober attendees. “It’s not anybody’s job—nor is it their right—to pry into the lives of their employees. But you should still make sure that you’re creating environments that are safe for people to be in,” Barbb says. “For executives and leaders, your responsibility for your people continues even outside of work hours.”.

Turning a design image into a working webpage can look simple.

You have a picture (a mockup, a screenshot, a Figma export), and your job is to turn it into working HTML in a browser.

But here is the catch. A design image is static, while a webpage is dynamic and responsive across different screen sizes and devices. A webpage needs to load quickly, adapt perfectly to different screen sizes, and allow touch interactions on mobile devices.

Most mistakes in this process happen when the conversion is treated as copying a picture instead of rebuilding it.

This section walks you through the mistakes developers often make, and more importantly, how to fix each of them.

Whether you are slicing a client mockup or converting a screenshot into code, avoiding these mistakes can save you from hours of rework. Let’s get into the details.

Sources indicate that A screenshot reflects how a page appears at a particular display. But it doesn’t show how the layout will behave when the content changes or the screen gets smaller.

Developers sometimes try to copy the exact positions and dimensions of every element. To match the screenshot, they may use fixed widths, large margins, and absolute positioning.

This can work at one screen size, but the layout may break on smaller screens or when a heading wraps onto an extra line.

According to recent reports, the better approach is identifying the layout rules behind the design. CSS Grid can arrange the cards in columns. Flexbox can help align elements within each card. And media queries can adjust the layout for smaller screens.

Pixel-level comparison can be useful in some cases, but it should not come at the cost of a flexible layout.

When developers recreate a design, it’s easier for them to focus on shapes and spacing rather than the purpose of each element. So, they may use generic elements for headings, buttons, navigation areas, and content sections instead of choosing elements that reflect each element's purpose.

This may produce the right appearance, but it often makes the code harder to maintain and understand. And when developers fail to use the right HTML elements, it can also create accessibility problems later.

Sources indicate that so don’t put everything inside several unnamed containers. Instead, use a clear structure with appropriate headings, meaningful alt text for informative images, and real buttons for actions.

Semantic elements (e.g., header, nav, main, section, and footer) can also help organize a large page when they match the content’s purpose.

A design image may have headings, descriptions, prices, labels, or button text.

Reusing the entire image to reproduce the original design feels quick. But it can create problems when that text has to work as part of a responsive web page.

Recent findings suggest that for example, there’s a promotional banner that contains a heading, a short description, and a CTA button. If you use the entire banner as one image, you can’t easily change the heading, translate the text, or make the button work as a real element.

So, don’t treat the image like that. Instead, use the original image where appropriate and recreate the text and button in HTML. CSS can control their position, size, color, and spacing.

Make sure you distinguish between visual elements that should remain images and text that should be recreated as HTML.

Not every part of turning images into HTML needs to be done manually.

Developers sometimes spend too much time on recreating basic elements when there are free online conversion tools available. These tools can help them get an initial version much faster.

An online conversion tool may be helpful when you need to extract text or generate a rough starting layout from a design image.

According to recent reports, for example, you can upload a design image into an online image to html converter to get a starting point (rather than starting from a blank file). Review the tool’s output. Identify the parts you can reuse (as they are) and tweak the parts that need adjustments.

Sources indicate that keep in mind that the first result generated by the tool isn’t the final code. You may need to reorganize the HTML, refine the CSS, and adjust the layout to make it responsive.

Use automation where it saves time and your own judgement where it matters.

Industry observers note that A screenshot demonstrates just one view of a page. It doesn’t show how the layout may change on a phone or how people using a keyboard/screen reader can interact with it.

So, developers who focus only on the desktop design may end up with:.

buttons that are difficult to use.

content that becomes too small on mobile devices.

There’s also a chance of accessibility problems when images lack suitable alt text/interactive elements.

In a recent development, let’s say a page has three cards in a row. On the desktop, this arrangement may work well. But on a phone, you may need to stack the cards vertically so their content remains readable.

It has been revealed that that’s why accessibility should be considered during the same process. Use meaningful headings and provide appropriate alt text for images. Also, maintain sufficient text contrast and make sure interactive elements can be operated with a keyboard.

Lastly, don’t forget to test the page on both desktop and mobile screen sizes before finalizing it.

HTML and CSS handle the structure and appearance of a webpage, but JavaScript makes it possible to add interactive features.

According to recent reports, for example, a design image may contain a navigation menu with a button. When recreating this design, developers should make sure the button performs an actual action rather than simply looking like a clickable element.

You can use JavaScript's event listeners to handle these interactions.

Now, add JavaScript to make the menu functional:.

In this example, clicking the button opens or closes the navigation menu. The aria-expanded attribute also communicates the menu's current state to assistive technologies.

In a recent development, this is a simple example of why converting a design image into HTML involves more than matching its appearance. Developers also need to recreate the behavior of interactive elements using appropriate HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

The process of turning an image into HTML feels easy when you treat it the right way.

Start by identifying the main sections, text, images, and interactive elements. Then create meaningful HTML and build the layout with CSS. Make the necessary adjustments to ensure it works across different screen sizes.

Sources indicate that use a conversion tool when it can really save time. But don’t forget to review the generated output of the tool thoroughly before using it.

A screenshot is a visual reference, not a complete set of development instructions. And the best result for you isn’t simply a page that looks like the image.

It is a page that also works well, adapts well, and stays easy to maintain.

Tech Report: Kagi, the paid Google Search alternative, now has a Gmail rival too

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kagi is best known as a paid alternative to Google Search, but the organization is now introducing its own email service that offers an alternative to Gmail.
  • Kagi Mail has been in the works for a long time, the organization notes in a post today, but it’s only just now launching in public beta.
  • In a recent development, there’s a 60-day trial for Kagi Mail, with the service costing $99.99/year (or included in Kagi’s $25/month Ultimate plan).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kagi is best known as a paid alternative to Google Search, but the organization is now introducing its own email service that offers an alternative to Gmail.

Kagi Mail has been in the works for a long time, the organization notes in a post today, but it’s only just now launching in public beta. Customers get an “@kagimail.com” address or can use their own domain, with both email and a calendar included.

In a recent development, there’s a 60-day trial for Kagi Mail, with the service costing $99.99/year (or included in Kagi’s $25/month Ultimate plan). The reason you’d pay that, Kagi explains, is because this is a product designed to “do its job and then get out of your way,” with no ads or “surveillance” as a part of the package.

Does the world need another email service? We asked ourselves that question more than once. There are great ones out there, and we’re fans of what Fastmail and Tuta are doing. We still built our own, for the same reason we build everything at Kagi: technology should do its job and then get out of your way.

For email, that job is to be fast, private, and secure. On top of that, it should help you stay on track with what’s important: bring forward what you need to act on, respond to, or acknowledge, and quietly handle the rest.

There’s a mobile app coming for Kagi Mail in early 2027, with a contact book and Kagi Assistant integration also slated for early next year. There is some natural language AI for organization, blocking of tracking pixels and remote images by default, and support for email clients like Apple Mail, and Kagi indicates everything can be exported to move to another provider should you choose.

Are you going to give it a try?

  • It has been revealed that if you have a smaller home that doesn't need the aid of wireless satellites to improve coverage, consider the TP-Link Archer BE230 Wi-Fi 7 router.
  • That price gets you 2.5 GbE WAN, four Gigabit LAN ports, and even a USB 3.0 port for adding storage to your network.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, black Friday Day 2026 is here, and we're already seeing some tasty deals on Wi-Fi routers. If you're in the market for a Wi-Fi 7 router, we've scoped out deals on standalone and mesh systems that could give your home (or office) network a much-needed performance boost.

It has been revealed that if you have a smaller home that doesn't need the aid of wireless satellites to improve coverage, consider the TP-Link Archer BE230 Wi-Fi 7 router. While it isn't one of TP-Link's most feature-packed Wi-Fi 7 offerings, it still offers a lot of bang for the buck. The Archer BE230 has a retail price of $119.99, but is at the moment just $74.99.

That price gets you 2.5 GbE WAN, four Gigabit LAN ports, and even a USB 3.0 port for adding storage to your network. The Archer AXE75 also supports EasyMesh, enabling you to combine multiple compatible routers into a mesh network.

Regarding performance, the Archer AXE75 operates at speeds of up to 688 Mbps on the 2.4 GHz band and up to 2,882 Mbps on the 5 GHz band.

The TP-Link Archer A230 is a value-priced dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router that features three GbE LAN ports and one 2.5 GbE WAN port.

If you need the added coverage of a mesh system, the TP-Link Deco BE63, which is a tri-band Wi-Fi 7 solution offering coverage of up to 5,800 square feet.

Each satellite has four 2.5 GbE ports, which are excellent for connecting your wired-only network devices, along with a single USB 3.0 port. However, there's another added benefit: the Deco BE63 supports wired backhaul, which can improve overall network performance compared to using the default wireless backhaul between satellites.

The Deco BE63 is typically available for $349.99, but is presently on sale for $279.99 for a two-pack.

The Deco BE63 is a mid-range, tri-band Wi-Fi 7 router with four 2.5 GbE ports, 10 Gbps of combined throughput, and coverage of 5,800 square feet.

Finally, on the TP-Link side, there's the Deco BE5000. This is an entry-level Wi-Fi 7 mesh router. Because of this alignment, the Deco BE5000 isn't a full-featured tri-band offering; instead, it's a dual-band Wi-Fi 7 solution. Although you miss out on the higher-performance 6 GHz band, you do gain support for Multi-Link Operation (MLO), a key pillar of Wi-Fi 7 (although MLO is one of Wi-Fi 7's most misunderstood features).

Each node features two 2.5 GbE ports, and you also get wired backhaul support. Maximum throughput reaches 688 Mbps for the 2.4 GHz band, while the 5 GHz band achieves 2,882 Mbps.

The Deco BE5000 retails for $299.99 but is right now priced at $198.19, which is a healthy $100 discount.

In a recent development, the TP-Link Deco BE5000 is a dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router that features three nodes and covers up to 6,600 square feet. Each node features 2.5 GbE ports and supports wired backhaul.

TP-Link isn't the only manufacturer doling out some enticing Wi-Fi 7 router discounts. If you're looking for a mid-range Wi-Fi 7 mesh router, the Netgear Orbi 770 is currently on sale for $424.99, which is sizable discount from its normal $549.99 asking price.

Sources indicate that the Orbi 700 Wi-Fi 7 mesh router is designed to envelope a spacious 5,500 square feet of space with peak speeds of up to 11 Gbps. These speedy routers come with three 2.5 GbE LAN ports and a single 2.5 GbE WAN port.

Industry observers note that the main router node features three 2.5 GbE LAN ports alongside a dedicated 2.5 GbE WAN port, whereas the satellite node provides two 2.5 GbE ports. Notably, neither unit includes a USB 3.x port, a feature that is becoming standard in this price range.

For wireless performance, the Orbi 770 supports speeds up to 688 Mbps on the 2.4 GHz band, 4,320 Mbps on 5 GHz, and 5,760 Mbps on 6 GHz. It provides coverage for up to 5,550 square feet—well above the average American home size of roughly 2,220 square feet. Network setup and management are available via Netgear's web interface or the Orbi mobile app.

Industry observers note that in our review of the three-node Orbi 770 system, we praised its user-friendly setup and generous port selection, though its high retail price remained a drawback. This Black Friday deal directly addresses that main concern.

In a recent development, netgear's Nighthawk RS90 is a dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router with a sleek exterior (aided by its internal antennas). It also has a full load of GbE and 2.5 GbE ports to support your wired client.

It has been revealed that the Netgear Nighthawk RS90 is priced at just $84.79 (15% off). It is a dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router, meaning that they don't include the higher-performance 6 GHz radio. While that means that short-range performance suffers compared to a tri-band router (when using a compatible Wi-Fi 7 or Wi-Fi 6E client), it allows for a much lower price.

The RS90 includes four GbE ports, one 2.5 GbE WAN port, and supports up to 2,000 square feet.

#161585. A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2297 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it?
  • In a recent development, researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself.
  • According to recent reports, the research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

In a recent development, researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

According to recent reports, the research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult.

Industry observers note that conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

In a recent development, "In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," states Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

It has been revealed that although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

Recent findings suggest that "Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal.

Industry observers note that the proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the upcoming approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information.

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

In a recent development, according to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

According to recent reports, "Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

In a recent development, this means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage.

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Industry observers note that ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect.".

In a recent development, the researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

According to recent reports, "Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," states Egues.

This behavior is notable because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor.

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Sources indicate that whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

Sources indicate that the nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

In a recent development, "We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small.".

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance.

In a recent development, in quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

Sources indicate that the approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy.

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

Recent findings suggest that however, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

Recent findings suggest that "All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely upcoming materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

Sources indicate that from a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising newly introduced way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.
